title: The AI-Scraping Free-for-All Is Coming to an End
summary: The AI-Scraping Free-for-All Is Coming to an End    MSN
editorial_override: AI-Scraping Free-for-All Is Coming to an End — core topic, scraping regulation tipping point
post_en:
The AI-scraping free-for-all is officially coming to an end.

New legal frameworks, court rulings, and platform defenses are converging to shut down unauthorized web data harvesting at scale.

What changed in 2026:
→ Major platforms now detect and block AI crawlers in real-time
→ Courts are ruling that AI training doesn't qualify as fair use by default
→ robots.txt is getting legal teeth — violating it now carries consequences
→ GDPR and CCPA regulators are treating unauthorized scraping as a data protection violation

For years, the AI industry operated on a simple assumption: if it's on the public web, it's fair game.

That assumption is dead.

The companies that will thrive are the ones already operating with:
• Licensed data partnerships
• Consent-based collection frameworks
• Transparent sourcing documentation
• Compliance infrastructure that scales across jurisdictions

The scraping era isn't over — but the era of scraping without rules is.

The question for every data team: is your pipeline built for the rules that exist today, or the ones that existed in 2023?

#WebScraping #DataCompliance #AITraining

Новые правовые рамки, судебные решения и защита платформ сходятся, чтобы остановить несанкционированный сбор веб-данных в масштабе.

Что изменилось в 2026:
→ Крупные платформы обнаруживают и блокируют AI-краулеры в реальном времени
→ Суды постановляют, что AI-обучение не является fair use по умолчанию
→ robots.txt получает юридическую силу — нарушение несёт последствия
→ Регуляторы GDPR и CCPA рассматривают несанкционированный скрейпинг как нарушение защиты данных

Годами AI-индустрия работала на простом допущении: если это в открытом вебе — это честная игра.

Это допущение мертво.

Эра скрейпинга не закончилась — закончилась эра скрейпинга без правил.

Вопрос для каждой data-команды: ваш пайплайн построен под правила 2026 или 2023 года?

#WebScraping #DataCompliance #AITraining

title: IP-Washing Methods in AI
summary: IP-Washing Methods in AI    Unite.AI
editorial_override: IP-Washing Methods in AI — directly about IP/proxy infrastructure in AI context
post_en:
IP-washing is becoming AI's dirty secret.

A new investigation reveals how AI companies launder their data collection through chains of proxies, VPNs, and intermediaries — making it impossible to trace what data was collected, from where, and with whose consent.

The playbook is disturbingly simple:
→ Route scrapers through multiple proxy layers
→ Use rotating residential IPs to avoid detection
→ Collect data through intermediary companies with no public connection to the AI lab
→ Mix licensed and unlicensed data to create plausible deniability

Sound familiar? It should. This is the same structure money laundering uses.

For the proxy infrastructure industry, this is a reckoning moment.

Providers can either:
1. Build compliance tools that prevent their infrastructure from being used for IP-washing
2. Or become the next industry that regulators dismantle

The legitimate data infrastructure market has always known this day was coming. Ethical sourcing, audit trails, and transparency aren't competitive advantages anymore.

They're survival requirements.

#DataEthics #AICompliance #ProxyInfrastructure

Новое расследование показывает, как AI-компании отмывают сбор данных через цепочки прокси, VPN и посредников — делая невозможным отслеживание того, какие данные собраны, откуда и с чьего согласия.

Плейбук пугающе прост:
→ Маршрутизация скрейперов через множество прокси-слоёв
→ Ротация резидентных IP для обхода детекции
→ Сбор данных через компании-посредники без публичной связи с AI-лабораторией
→ Смешивание лицензированных и нелицензированных данных

Звучит знакомо? Это та же структура, что использует отмывание денег.

Для прокси-индустрии это момент истины. Провайдеры могут либо строить инструменты compliance, либо стать следующей индустрией, которую разберут регуляторы.

Этичное происхождение, аудит-трейлы и прозрачность — уже не конкурентные преимущества. Это требования для выживания.

title: Google's Scraping Suit Asks How Far DMCA Protections Go
summary: Google's Scraping Suit Asks How Far DMCA Protections Go    Law360
editorial_override: Google scraping suit: how far DMCA protections go — legal precedent for web scraping
post_en:
Google's latest scraping lawsuit is asking a question that could reshape the entire web data industry:

How far do DMCA protections actually go?

The case tests whether DMCA's anti-circumvention provisions apply when scrapers bypass technical protection measures like rate limiting, CAPTCHAs, and access controls.

If the court rules broadly, every scraper that bypasses a rate limit or solves a CAPTCHA could face DMCA liability — not just copyright infringement claims.

What this means for data teams:
→ Technical access controls may become legally protected barriers, not just speed bumps
→ The distinction between "publicly available" and "freely accessible" gets a legal definition
→ Proxy infrastructure used to circumvent protections could face secondary liability
→ Legitimate data access partnerships become the only safe path at scale

The web scraping industry has long argued that public data is public data. Courts are starting to disagree.

Whether you're scraping or building anti-scraping tools, this case will define the rules for the next decade.

#WebScraping #DMCA #DataAccess
post_ru:
Новый иск Google о скрейпинге задаёт вопрос, который может перестроить всю индустрию веб-данных:

Как далеко реально распространяется защита DMCA?

Дело проверяет, применяются ли положения DMCA против обхода технических мер защиты — rate limiting, CAPTCHA, контроля доступа.

Если суд примет широкое решение, каждый скрейпер, обходящий rate limit или CAPTCHA, может получить DMCA-ответственность.

Что это значит:
→ Технические барьеры доступа могут стать юридически защищёнными
→ Различие между «публично доступным» и «свободно доступным» получит юридическое определение
→ Прокси-инфраструктура для обхода защит может нести вторичную ответственность

Индустрия скрейпинга долго утверждала: публичные данные — публичные. Суды начинают не соглашаться.

#WebScraping #DMCA #DataAccess

title: Your favorite image-saving Chrome extension was scraping your data for cash
summary: Your favorite image-saving Chrome extension was scraping your data for cash    9to5Google
editorial_override: Chrome extension scraping user data for cash — data privacy violation, scraping abuse
post_en:
Your favorite Chrome extension was selling your browsing data. Yes, that one.

A popular image-saving extension with millions of users was caught scraping browsing history, search queries, and page content — then selling the data to third-party brokers.

The extension operated for years before detection. Users never knew.

This is the shadow data economy in action:
→ Browser extensions have access to EVERYTHING you do online
→ Most users never read permissions beyond "this extension needs access to websites"
→ Data brokers pay premium prices for real human browsing patterns
→ The data ends up training AI models, building ad profiles, and feeding competitive intelligence

For anyone in the data infrastructure business, this is a cautionary tale:

The line between data collection and data theft isn't technical — it's about consent.

Ethical data companies must be able to answer: Does the user know? Did they agree? Can they opt out?

If your data pipeline can't answer those three questions for every data point, you're one investigation away from this headline.

#DataPrivacy #BrowserSecurity #DataEthics

Популярное расширение для сохранения изображений с миллионами пользователей пойманона скрейпинге истории просмотров, поисковых запросов и контента страниц — с продажей данных брокерам.

→ Брокеры данных платят премиум за реальные паттерны просмотра
→ Данные попадают в AI-модели, рекламные профили и competitive intelligence

Граница между сбором данных и кражей данных — не техническая. Это вопрос согласия.

Знает ли пользователь? Согласился ли? Может ли отказаться?

#DataPrivacy #BrowserSecurity #DataEthics

title: Introducing the Fingerprint MCP Server: the AI interface for device intelligence
summary: The Fingerprint MCP Server connects any AI agent to your device intelligence data, enabling fraud teams to investigate suspicious activity, detect anomalies, and analyze events using natural language in seconds instead of hours.
editorial_override: Fingerprint MCP Server: AI interface for device intelligence — fingerprinting/bot detection tech
post_en:
Fingerprint just launched an MCP server — making device intelligence directly accessible to AI agents.

This is a bigger deal than it sounds.

Until now, device fingerprinting required custom API integrations. Now any AI agent that speaks MCP can:
→ Identify returning visitors across sessions
→ Detect bot vs. human traffic in real-time
→ Score risk based on device and network signals
→ Block fraud before it reaches your application layer

Why this matters for the data infrastructure industry:

Device intelligence is moving from "security feature" to "infrastructure layer."

When AI agents can natively query fingerprint data, every automated interaction becomes identifiable. This changes the economics of bot detection fundamentally.

For proxy providers: the bar just went up. AI-powered detection that queries device intelligence in real-time means static proxy rotation is no longer enough.

For data teams: this is the clearest signal yet that the web is moving toward an identity-first access model. Anonymous scraping at scale becomes harder every quarter.

The question isn't whether device intelligence becomes standard. It's whether your infrastructure is ready for it.

#DeviceIntelligence #BotDetection #AIAgents

title: 'Pokémon Go' players unknowingly trained delivery robots with 30B images
summary: Article URL: https://www.popsci.com/technology/pokemon-go-delivery-robots-crowdsourcing/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47398479 Points: 110 # Comments: 61
editorial_override: Pokémon Go players unknowingly trained robots with 30B images — massive data collection ethics
post_en:
30 billion images. Collected from Pokémon Go players. Used to train delivery robots.

Players walked around capturing Pokémon. The game captured their surroundings. Now those images train autonomous delivery systems.

Nobody told the players.

This is the most important data ethics story of the month — and nobody is talking about it.

The implications are massive:
→ Every AR/VR app is a potential data collection pipeline
→ "Gameplay data" can include environmental scanning, biometric patterns, and movement data
→ Consent for "playing a game" ≠ consent for "training commercial AI systems"
→ This data was collected at a scale no dedicated data company could match

For the data industry, this raises a fundamental question:

When does user-generated data become training data without consent?

The companies that will define the next era of data infrastructure aren't the ones collecting the most data. They're the ones that can prove every data point was collected with informed consent.

30 billion images. Zero informed consent. That's not a business model — it's a lawsuit waiting to happen.

#DataEthics #AITraining #Privacy

→ Каждое AR/VR-приложение — потенциальный data collection pipeline
→ «Игровые данные» включают сканирование среды, биометрику и данные перемещений
→ Согласие на «игру» ≠ согласие на «обучение коммерческих AI-систем»

title: Conseil d'État upholds Criteo's €40M GDPR fine
summary: Conseil d'État upholds Criteo's €40M GDPR fine    noyb.eu
editorial_override: Criteo €40M GDPR fine upheld by Conseil d'État — GDPR enforcement precedent
post_en:
France's highest administrative court just upheld Criteo's €40 million GDPR fine.

No reduction. No technicality. Full enforcement.

This is significant because Criteo isn't some obscure startup — it's one of the largest ad tech companies in Europe. And the fine targets the core of the behavioral advertising model.

The violations:
→ Collecting browsing data without valid consent
→ Failing to demonstrate a legitimate interest for tracking
→ Inadequate transparency about how user data flowed through the ad tech chain

What makes this ruling different:
→ It survived the highest possible appeal — this is now settled law
→ It targets the ad tech intermediary, not just the publisher
→ It sets a precedent that "everyone in ad tech does this" is not a defense

For anyone building data products that involve user tracking, browsing data, or cross-site analytics:

The Criteo ruling proves that GDPR enforcement has teeth — and those teeth reach the entire data supply chain, not just the company facing the user.

#GDPR #AdTech #DataPrivacy

Criteo — один из крупнейших ad tech в Европе. Штраф бьёт в ядро модели поведенческой рекламы.

Нарушения:
→ Сбор данных просмотра без валидного согласия

title: Public Forum: Internet Scraping and the Future of the Open Web in the Internet Age -
summary: Public Forum: Internet Scraping and the Future of the Open Web in the Internet Age    - Center for Democracy and Technology
editorial_override: Public Forum: Internet Scraping and Future of Open Web — scraping policy debate
post_en:
A major public forum just asked the question the entire data industry has been avoiding:

"What is the future of the open web in the age of internet scraping?"

The forum brought together regulators, publishers, tech companies, and data infrastructure providers to address:

→ Should websites have enforceable rights against automated data collection?
→ Does the "open web" principle conflict with data protection laws?
→ How should legitimate data needs (research, AI training, competitive intelligence) be balanced against content creators' rights?
→ What role should proxy infrastructure play in regulated data access?

The conversation signals a shift from "should we regulate scraping" to "how do we regulate scraping."

3 takeaways for data teams:
1. Self-regulation is ending — formal frameworks are coming
2. Technical access ≠ legal access (this will be codified)
3. Data infrastructure providers will be part of the regulatory conversation

The open web isn't closing. But "open" is getting a new definition — one that includes rules about who can access it, how, and for what purpose.

#WebScraping #OpenWeb #DataRegulation
post_ru:

«Каково будущее открытого веба в эпоху интернет-скрейпинга?»

Регуляторы, паблишеры, tech-компании и провайдеры data-инфраструктуры обсудили:
→ Должны ли сайты иметь исполнимые права против автоматического сбора данных?
→ Конфликтует ли принцип «открытого веба» с законами о защите данных?
→ Как балансировать легитимные потребности в данных с правами создателей контента?

Разговор сместился от «надо ли регулировать скрейпинг» к «как регулировать скрейпинг».

Открытый веб не закрывается. Но «открытый» получает новое определение — с правилами о том, кто может получить доступ, как и зачем.

#WebScraping #OpenWeb #DataRegulation

title: Why using corporate IPs for research is risky
summary: Why using corporate IPs for research is risky    Cybernews
editorial_override: Why using corporate IPs for research is risky — competitor_watch, proxy/IP topic
post_en:
"We'll just use our corporate IPs for web research."

I hear this from enterprise data teams more than you'd think. Here's why it's one of the riskiest decisions you can make:

→ Your corporate IP gets flagged → your entire company loses access to target platforms
→ Aggressive crawling from a corporate range triggers legal attention, not just rate limits
→ You're creating a forensic trail that directly links scraping activity to your organization
→ One overeager intern can get your company banned from a critical data source permanently

The false economy of "saving money" on proxy infrastructure:
• $0/month on proxies
• $50,000 in legal fees when you receive a cease-and-desist
• Permanent loss of access to data you need for competitive intelligence
• Your company name in a public court filing about unauthorized scraping

This is why data infrastructure exists. It's not just about IP rotation — it's about separating research activity from corporate identity, managing request patterns, and maintaining access over time.

The cheapest solution is always the most expensive when it fails.

#DataInfrastructure #WebResearch #ProxyInfrastructure
post_ru:
«Мы просто используем корпоративные IP для веб-исследований.»

Слышу это от enterprise data-команд чаще, чем вы думаете. Почему это одно из самых рискованных решений:

→ Корпоративный IP попадает в бан → вся компания теряет доступ к целевым платформам
→ Агрессивный кроулинг с корпоративного диапазона вызывает юридическое внимание
→ Создаёте forensic trail, связывающий скрейпинг напрямую с организацией
→ Один неосторожный стажёр может навсегда забанить компанию

Ложная экономия «экономии» на прокси-инфраструктуре:
• $0/мес на прокси
• $50,000 на юристов при получении cease-and-desist
• Потеря доступа к данным для competitive intelligence

Data-инфраструктура существует не только для ротации IP — это разделение исследовательской активности и корпоративной идентичности.

#DataInfrastructure #WebResearch #ProxyInfrastructure

title: Build your own MCP server: LLMs meets web data with Zyte API

editorial_override: Build MCP server with Zyte API — competitor Zyte, web data infrastructure
post_en:
Zyte just launched an MCP server that connects LLMs directly to web data extraction.

This means AI agents can now instruct a web scraping pipeline in natural language — no custom code required.

Why this matters more than another API launch:

The MCP (Model Context Protocol) standard is becoming the bridge between AI agents and the physical web. When scraping infrastructure speaks MCP, every AI agent becomes a potential data consumer.

What this changes:
→ The barrier to web data collection drops to zero (just ask an AI in plain English)
→ Scale increases dramatically — agents can orchestrate thousands of extractions
→ Quality control becomes critical because agents don't inherently understand data quality
→ Compliance complexity multiplies when non-technical users can launch scrapers

The web data industry is about to get a LOT bigger — and a lot more chaotic.

The winners won't be the companies with the best extraction technology. They'll be the ones with the best guardrails: compliance checks, quality filtering, and ethical sourcing built into the pipeline.

When everyone can scrape, the value shifts from access to trust.

#WebData #AIAgents #MCP

title: Canada's bill C-22 mandates mass metadata surveillance
summary: https://www.parl.ca/DocumentViewer/en/45-1/bill/C-22/first-r... Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47392084 Points: 928 # Comments: 291
editorial_override: Canada bill C-22 mandates mass metadata surveillance — surveillance/privacy regulation
post_en:
Canada just introduced Bill C-22 — mandating mass metadata surveillance of all internet communications.

ISPs would be required to collect and retain:
→ IP addresses and connection timestamps
→ Email metadata (who emailed who, when)
→ Web browsing patterns and DNS queries
→ Device identifiers and location data

No warrant required for access by law enforcement.

The implications for the data industry are enormous:

When governments mandate metadata collection, they create the largest surveillance databases on earth. And these databases become targets — for hackers, for authoritarian overreach, and for function creep.

For anyone operating data infrastructure:
→ VPN and proxy usage will spike as privacy-conscious users route around surveillance
→ Enterprise data teams need to understand which jurisdictions their traffic touches
→ The line between "network security logging" and "surveillance infrastructure" disappears

Every country that mandates mass metadata collection eventually uses it beyond its original scope. Every single one.

The question isn't whether this data will be misused. It's when.

#DataPrivacy #Surveillance #InternetFreedom
post_ru:

ISP обязаны собирать и хранить:
→ IP-адреса и временные метки соединений
→ Метаданные email
→ Паттерны веб-просмотра и DNS-запросы
→ Идентификаторы устройств и данные геолокации

Без ордера для доступа правоохранителей.

Когда правительства обязывают собирать метаданные, они создают крупнейшие базы данных слежки на Земле. И эти базы становятся целями.

→ VPN и прокси-использование вырастет
→ Enterprise-командам нужно понимать, каких юрисдикций касается их трафик
→ Граница между логированием и инфраструктурой слежки исчезает

Каждая страна, обязавшая массовый сбор метаданных, в итоге использует его за пределами первоначального назначения. Каждая.

#DataPrivacy #Surveillance #InternetFreedom

title: Show HN: OpenLegion – AI agent fleet with container isolation and vault proxy
summary: I built OpenLegion because every AI agent framework I tried had the same problems in production: API keys sitting in config files inside the agent's environment, no way to set hard spend limits, and LLM-as-CEO task routing that's non-deterministic and unauditable. The short version of what I built: Security: Every agent runs in its own Docker container or microVM. A vault proxy sits between agents and every LLM call — the agent sends a request, the proxy injects the credential at the network layer, the agent gets back a response. Keys never exist inside the container. Six independent security layers on by default, including per-agent ACL matrices and Unicode sanitization to block invisible-character prompt injection. Cost control: Per-agent daily and monthly budgets with a hard cutoff enforced at the vault proxy. The agent physically cannot make an LLM call that exceeds its budget. Zero markup on LLM usage — you pay your provider directly at their rates. 100+ providers via LiteLLM with configurable failover chains. Orchestration: Deterministic YAML DAG workflows. No LLM deciding what runs next. Four patterns: sequential, parallel, supervisor, hierarchical. Every execution path is predictable and auditable.
